newsitem.title: CHINA: China leader sees state firm reform as problem.
newsitem.headline: China leader sees state firm reform as problem.

text.p: The challenge of transforming lumbering state enterprises into firms lean enough to compete in a sink-or-swim marketplace is among China's most pressing problems, Vice Premier Li Lanqing said.
The challenge would result in the elimination of firms that failed to restructure or to abandon the cushion of central planning, he said in an interview this week.
"For example, there is a river and on this bank is the traditional planned economy and on the other bank is the socialist market economy," he told Reuters.
"There is a bridge across this river," he said. "Some enterprises have already crossed this bridge...some are still on the bridge and some remain on this side.
"What we are trying to do is to enable more enterprises to cross the bridge," he said. "Of course, some enterprises will not be able to cross and will just drop into the river."

Chinese officials have conceded problems in reforming some 100,000 state enterprises, of which an estimated 70 percent are loss-making or chronically in the red while the number that have simply ceased production has been rising this year.
Vice Premier Li outlined a string of problems that needed to be solved if more state-owned enterprises, cushioned for years by state subsidies, were to cross the bridge.
Many state firms were burdened by having to provide cradle-to-grave social security for all staff and their families, Li said.

"The traditional planned economy did not have a social security system and state enterprises were greatly burdened because they take care of workers in every aspect," Li said, referring to the "iron rice bowl" that paramount leader Deng Xiaoping's 17-year-old economic reforms are intended to smash.

"They had to take care of everything from kindergarten to university," Li said, joking that when he had been responsible for running such an enterprise, one of his odder tasks had been to find a way to speed up the queue for the company barber.

In addition, state firms had difficulty adjusting to the 1985 introduction of bank loans rather than state subsidies. As a result, many firms -- some of them efficient and producing marketable products -- could not pay principle or interest, he said.

However, problems facing the enterprises -- which one senior official this year compared to pampered caged tigers that would have difficulty hunting for food if set free in the wild -- extended beyond the purely commercial sphere.
Li detailed the difficulties of teaching officials accustomed to decades of central planning how to compete.
"Some people can't adapt their mindset to the new socialist market economy," he said.

"They do not look into the market mood and study what the market needs. They hope that whatever they produce can be sold," Li said. "But now the problem is that the people do not llke their products and they do not buy."
China's state sector reported a net loss of 3.0 billion yuan ($361 million) in the first quarter of this year, the first such deficit since Deng launched reforms in 1979.
The latest figures showed that industries under the central government reported a total profit of 22.636 billion yuan in the first nine months, slumping by 28.5 percent from last year.
However, losses soared 23.0 percent to 14.101 billion yuan, according to figures issued by the State Statistical Bureau.
